entrance.text: Your party of four stands before the crumbling entrance to an old dungeon. Torchlight flickers somewhere deep inside.
entrance.guide: Every Four Against Darkness adventure starts right here, at the dungeon door. The game unfolds in turns: each one presents a situation and asks you to choose an action — exactly what you're about to do below.

corridor_fork.text: Just inside, the corridor splits: one way flickers with torchlight, the other is shrouded in quiet darkness. Exploration is part of the adventure — different paths lead to different risks.
corridor_fork.guide: Choices like this show up constantly in FAD — the game often hands you multiple routes with different risk levels and lets you decide. There's no single correct answer, just like at the tabletop.

quiet_passage.text: You creep through the dark passage undetected. No traps here — but you can't be sure what's waiting ahead either.
quiet_passage.guide: This turn resolved with no roll and no cost — a stand-in for a random room draw that turns out uneventful. Not every turn in the real game needs a fight or a trap; some are just progress.

corridor_trap.text: The corridor floor is covered in strange tiles. One looks slightly loose — it might be a pressure-plate trap. This is your first lesson: not every hazard needs to be fought.
corridor_trap.guide: This is a Trap turn. The rulebook usually resolves traps with a skill check; here your choice stands in for that check. Caution is almost always the safer play against a hazard you haven't identified.

trap_avoided.text: You spot the trigger and step over it safely. The party presses on unharmed.
trap_avoided.guide: No roll, no cost — spotting a hazard by paying attention is free in FAD. Compare this outcome to the alternate path; that's the kind of trade-off traps are built around.

trap_triggered.text: The tile clicks. A dart shoots from the wall and catches one of your heroes! A small price for the lesson: always check for traps.
trap_triggered.guide: Triggering a trap cost your party 1 HP on a random hero. This is FAD's core risk/reward loop in miniature: rushing forward is tempting, but it spends a resource (HP) you'll want later.

goblin_room.text: Two goblins turn and snarl at you. They are Level 3 minions. Combat, bribery, and fleeing are all valid tactics — Four Against Darkness rewards good judgement over brute force.
goblin_room.guide: This is a full Encounter turn — the heart of the game. You have three standard responses: Fight (roll to resolve combat), Bribe (spend gold to skip the fight entirely), or Flee (retreat and try a different approach). All three are equally legitimate strategies.

goblin_fight_resolution.text: You roll to attack and the goblins fall before your blades! The path ahead is clear.
goblin_fight_resolution.guide: You resolved combat with a single attack roll (needing 4+ on a d6) for the whole party. The full rulebook runs combat in rounds with each hero rolling separately — this tutorial simplifies that down to one roll so the lesson stays clear.

goblin_fight_setback.text: Your attack goes wide and a goblin's blade catches one of your heroes before you finish them off. Combat always carries risk — that's why bribery and fleeing are on the table too.
goblin_fight_setback.guide: A failed attack roll still costs you — here, 1 HP to a random hero. This is exactly why Bribe and Flee exist as real alternatives, not just flavor options: combat in FAD is never a guaranteed win.

goblin_bribe_success.text: The goblins snatch the gold and scurry off, leaving the path clear without a single blow struck.
goblin_bribe_success.guide: Bribing trades gold for safety instead of risking HP. It's a completely legitimate FAD tactic — sometimes the smartest play is to not fight at all.

goblin_flee.text: You beat a hasty retreat back down the corridor, goblins hooting behind you. Fleeing is always an option when the odds look bad — regrouping and trying another approach beats a bad fight.
goblin_flee.guide: Fleeing costs you a turn but nothing else — no HP, no gold. In FAD, retreating from a bad fight and regrouping is always on the table; living to try again beats a costly win.

treasure_room.text: Beyond the goblins lies a small chest and a shimmering rune etched into the far wall.
treasure_room.guide: Clearing an encounter often reveals Treasure — FAD's reward loop for taking the risk. If your party includes a Wizard, you'll also see a class-specific option here; certain challenges favor certain classes, which is part of why party composition matters during Setup.

magic_lesson.text: Your Wizard channels arcane energy to decipher the rune, revealing a hidden catch on the chest. Magic can solve problems combat cannot.
magic_lesson.guide: Magic-using classes can interact with the world in ways others can't — here, your Wizard solves a puzzle with no roll and no risk. This is why a well-rounded party often out-performs four heroes of the same class.

treasure_found.text: Inside the chest: a stash of gold, split evenly among your party, and a masterwork dagger tucked beneath it. Tutorial complete — you've learned the basics: combat, traps, fleeing, and magic.
treasure_found.guide: You've now played the full loop that makes up every FAD turn: face a situation, choose an action, deal with the consequences, and claim the reward. The complete game repeats this pattern across many more rooms, encounters, and dungeon levels than this tutorial covers.

party_wiped.text: Your entire party has fallen. Four Against Darkness is unforgiving that way — but every defeat is a lesson for the next attempt.
party_wiped.guide: A full party wipe ends the adventure, but Four Against Darkness is built to be replayed quickly — restarting with a different strategy is part of the experience, not a failure.
